transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed
today that the U.S. military will cut 20 percent of its generals and admirals, NPR's
Tom Bowman reports.
Secretary Hegseth said he plans a sharp cut in the number of generals and admirals. He's
long complained about a blow to bureaucracy, politically correct officers. Now, get this,
there are some 850 of these senior officers, which has jumped 31 percent in the last five
decades. Here's what he said.
You see, the number crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across
the force. And that number sounds about right. And I know because I directed it that we've
also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent.
So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board.
Some retired officers I talk with say, you know, listen, we're probably too top-heavy
with senior military leaders, but they worry whether this will be done appropriately, will
Hegseth, let's say, try to get rid of officers he sees as not loyal.
NPR's Tom Bowman reporting. Cornell University says the school will cooperate with an independent
investigation of the handling of an alleged sexual assault in 2024 after New York Governor
Kathy Hochul demanded the probe. NPR's Brian Mann reports a prosecutor says he's trying
to schedule a meeting with the woman at the center of the case.
In the woman's 2024 statement to campus police, she described swatting a man's hand away from
her genitals and resisting an unwanted kiss from another man all while she was heavily
intoxicated. Still, D.A. Matthew Van Houten determined the incident was consensual. But
now after seeing detailed accusations of a gang rape laid out in her civil lawsuit, Van
Houten says he's working to arrange a first meeting with the alleged victim.
It will be a process that takes some time, as much time as she needs. And we need to
make sure we understand everything and have all the evidence.
Cornell's student government, meanwhile, is holding a hearing on the case Friday after
condemning the university's response. Brian Mann, NPR News at The Good New York.
President Trump this week again said he wants to send most American adults $5,000 checks
if Republicans keep control of the House and Senate. NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben reports
it's just one way he's proposed increasing the government's economic reach while railing
against communism. Trump's idea drew criticism from even some
allies at first. His government has also taken equity stakes in private companies, imposed
dozens of tariffs and taken the unusual step of trying to lower interest rates via the
Treasury Department. It raises a contradiction ahead of the midterms. Trump continues to
label Democrats communists and socialists and is the leader of the party that claims
to support free markets while he tries to bend the economy to his will.
Trump's message was further muddied when he last week hosted a state dinner for Chinese
President Xi Jinping and made a friendly appearance with New York City Mayor Zoran Mamdani, who
is a Democratic socialist. Danielle Kurtzleben, NPR News.
Most U.S. stocks fell today. This is NPR News.
The Supreme Court is allowing the execution of Christa Gail Pike in Tennessee to go forward.
The ruling overturns a last-minute stay issued by a lower court. Pike admitted to killing
a classmate when she was 18. An appeals court ruled that a delay was needed to consider
Pike's claims of childhood sexual abuse. This would be Tennessee's first execution
of a woman in over 200 years. An NPR investigation finds children with disabilities are the largest
group in foster care and they have the worst outcomes in foster care. NPR's Joseph Shapiro
reports.
NPR obtained data on a half million children and youth in foster care. Our analysis found
that disabled kids stay in foster care the longest, 50 percent longer than other children.
They're more likely to be moved from place to place and they're far more likely to live
in institutional settings rather than with a foster family. Another study found foster
kids with physical disabilities are nine times more likely to die. Nancy Thaler leads a federally
funded program to improve care for kids with tricky behavioral health issues, kids who
sometimes hurt themselves or others. This is the group that everybody gives up on
and it's because they have disabilities. But Thaler says new brain science shows these
kids can recover and lead successful lives. Joseph Shapiro, NPR News. A gray shark named
Bukangi has become an honorary mascot in South Korea's port city of Busan, but guiding it
back to open water has been tricky. Five vessels were deployed yesterday but the crews gave
up after hours of unsuccessfully spraying streams of water to hurt the shark toward
the open sea. This is NPR.

topics.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirms U.S. military will cut 20 percent of generals and admirals
Cornell University agrees to independent investigation of alleged 2024 sexual assault after Governor Hochul demands probe
President Trump proposes sending most American adults $5,000 checks if Republicans keep House and Senate control
Supreme Court allows execution of Christa Gail Pike in Tennessee to proceed, first woman execution in 200 years
NPR investigation finds children with disabilities are largest group in foster care with worst outcomes
Gray shark Bukangi in South Korea's Busan port resists efforts to guide it back to open water
